paras: The lynching of Joe Caleb took place on the night of August 31, 1881, when a party of armed men took Caleb, a young Black man held on a charge of attempting to burn a house, from the jail at Vernon in Jackson Parish, Louisiana, and hanged him beside the Trenton road. Caleb had been accused of setting fire to the house of T. J. Fuller the previous April while thirteen people were inside. An inquest failed to identify the lynchers, and a New Orleans Item editorial said it could "hardly blame" them.

According to the Columbia Herald, citing District Attorney George Wear, Fuller's house was set on fire on the night of April 2, 1881, with coal oil poured around it in six places. Thirteen people were inside, and articles stolen from the house that night were found in an adjoining field. Suspicion fell on two Black people, Joe Caleb and a woman named Mattie Larchie, and the Herald judged the evidence against Caleb strong because tracks found at the house "corresponded with his."

Both were jailed after a preliminary examination, but Caleb broke jail before he could be indicted. Larchie was tried at the August term of the district court, and her jury failed to agree, standing eleven for conviction and one for acquittal. Caleb was rearrested in late August and jailed at Vernon.

On Wednesday night, August 31, a party of men described in a letter to Wear as "unknown" came to the Vernon jail and captured deputy sheriffs James and Mack Smith, who were sleeping there. The men took the keys from the deputies, opened the door and led Caleb out under a strong guard. They carried him down the Trenton road to a point below "the Hon. E. E. Kidd's" and hanged him from a limb at the roadside. The other prisoners in the jail were not harmed.
The Claiborne Guardian called the lynchers "a mob of armed men"; no report gave their number.

An inquest was held, but according to the letter to Wear it obtained "nothing definite" about who the lynchers were. No report of arrests, indictments or a trial of anyone in the lynching appears in the coverage. In October the Donaldsonville Chief reported that Mattie Larchie was still held for trial as an alleged confederate in the arson.

The lynching was reported in white newspapers, mostly Louisiana weeklies that passed it along in columns of state news. The first known report, in the Claiborne Guardian of Homer on September 14, and the Bossier Banner the next day both asserted that Caleb had confessed. A National Associated Press dispatch from Shreveport, printed in the Omaha Daily Bee on September 17 under the headline "Lynched to a Tree Limb," stated as fact that Caleb had set the fire and had been "arrested and convicted."

The Baton Rouge Louisiana Capitolian reprinted the Herald's account twice. The Herald wrote that this mode of dealing with prisoners was "to be strongly deprecated" and that a jury could have rendered justice, but it closed by calling the deed "daring—desperate—fiendish." The Richland Beacon of Rayville took a sharper line, writing that the case showed "to what lengths" mobs would go and how dangerous they were to any community.

The fullest commentary came from the New Orleans Item, reprinted in the Ouachita Telegraph of Monroe on September 23 under the heading "Louisiana Lynch-Law." The Item called the alleged arson "a peculiarly fiendish one" and argued that Caleb might have been acquitted "through the stupidity or partizanship of a mixed jury." It held that in parts of Louisiana "the whites must rule with a rod of iron" and concluded that, although the lynchers may have acted "overhastily," it could "hardly blame them if they were positive that they had the right man."

The Shreveport dispatch said Caleb had been convicted, while the Herald, citing the district attorney, said he escaped before indictment; the Herald's is the more detailed account and comes from the prosecutor. The Guardian and the Banner said he had confessed, but the Herald's account mentions no confession. The Donaldsonville Chief alone gave his name as "Joe Cable."

framing.detail: The Claiborne Guardian and Bossier Banner ran one-sentence items asserting Caleb had 'confessed', without comment on the mob.
The Columbia Herald called the method 'strongly deprecated' but ended on the 'horrible' alleged arson, 'daring—desperate—fiendish'.
The Omaha Daily Bee ran the Shreveport dispatch under 'Lynched to a Tree Limb', presenting the arson and a conviction as fact.
The Richland Beacon said the case 'shows to what lengths' mobs go and how dangerous they are to any community.
The New Orleans Item, reprinted in the Ouachita Telegraph as 'Louisiana Lynch-Law', said whites 'must rule with a rod of iron' and it could 'hardly blame' the lynchers.
